Syntactic Structure & Grammatical Form: Fixed declarative clause with fronted relative/interrogative pronoun; modal verb mutt repeated elliptically.
Figurative Meaning (Contextualized Defin: Something necessary must be done, even if it is unpleasant or inconvenient.
Non-Idiomatic Equivalent (Plain, Neutral: Dat is nödig, also maakt wi dat.
Usage Contexts: daily speech; work; family duties; pragmatic encouragement
Cultural Origin or Historical Reference: Strongly associated with northern German and Low Saxon pragmatism; often used when work, weather, or duty leaves little room for complaint.
First Example Sentence: Wat mutt, dat mutt, seggt Opa, as wi bi Regen den Tuun wedder fastmaken.
Second Example Sentence: Ik harr keen Lust op de Versammeln, man wat mutt, dat mutt.
Third Example Sentence: De Melk mutt na de Markt, wat mutt, dat mutt.

Syntactic Structure & Grammatical Form: Two coordinated main clauses; negative imperative plus demonstrative-subject declarative.
Figurative Meaning (Contextualized Defin: Stop talking or complaining and try it; the task is possible.
Non-Idiomatic Equivalent (Plain, Neutral: Höör op to klagen; du kannst dat schaffen.
Usage Contexts: workshop talk; family; sports; practical problem-solving; friendly teasing
Cultural Origin or Historical Reference: A well-known northern saying, especially recognizable in Hamburg-style everyday speech, reflecting hands-on maritime and craft culture.
First Example Sentence: Sabbel nich, dat geiht, wenn du den Knoop eerst richtig fasttreckst.
Second Example Sentence: As de Lehrjung bang vör de Maschien weer, sä de Meister: Sabbel nich, dat geiht.
Third Example Sentence: Wi hebbt nich veel Tiet; sabbel nich, dat geiht.

Syntactic Structure & Grammatical Form: Elliptical predicative phrase; indefinite pronoun plus prepositional phrase without finite verb.
Figurative Meaning (Contextualized Defin: Everything is fine, settled, or under control.

Cultural Origin or Historical Reference: Botter evokes everyday dairy and household abundance in northern rural life; the phrase signals that nothing is spoiled or lacking.
First Example Sentence: Maak di keen Sorgen, mit de Rechnung is allens in Botter.
Second Example Sentence: Na de Reparatur löppt de Pomp wedder, allens in Botter.
Third Example Sentence: Ik heff mit Anna snackt, twüschen uns is allens in Botter.

Syntactic Structure & Grammatical Form: Negative declarative clause; idiomatic animal subject with verb of sound and locative-adverbial complement.
Figurative Meaning (Contextualized Defin: Nobody will care, notice, or complain about it.

Second Example Sentence: Se maakt ut de lütte Pann een Drama, aver keen Hahn kreiht dor na.
Third Example Sentence: Laat den Olen Weg so, keen Hahn kreiht dor na.

Syntactic Structure & Grammatical Form: Locative-presentational clause with expletive-locative adverb; perfect participle adjective in passive-like construction.
Figurative Meaning (Contextualized Defin: That is the real problem, hidden cause, or decisive point.

Cultural Origin or Historical Reference: A broadly northern and Germanic metaphor of finding the buried matter; in Low Saxon speech it often marks the practical core of a problem.

Second Example Sentence: Dat Geld fehlt nich, dor liggt de Hund begraven bi de Planung.
Third Example Sentence: Se snackt üm den Brei, man dor liggt de Hund begraven: he hett keen Tiet.

Third Example Sentence: Holl den Kopp in'n Wind, denn kummt de Dag ok wedder lichter.

Idiom (Low Saxon): De Appel fallt nich wiet vun'n Stamm.
Syntactic Structure & Grammatical Form: Fixed proverb-like declarative clause; noun subject, negated adverbial distance, prepositional source phrase.
Figurative Meaning (Contextualized Defin: Children often resemble their parents in character, habits, or talent.
Non-Idiomatic Equivalent (Plain, Neutral: Dat Kind is sien Öllern bannig liek.
Cultural Origin or Historical Reference: Agrarian tree imagery is common in Low Saxon proverbs; the apple-and-tree metaphor links kinship to visible rural experience.

First Example Sentence: Lena kan so good snacken as ehr Vader; de Appel fallt nich wiet vun'n Stamm.
Second Example Sentence: As Jan wedder an de Trecker schruuvt, lacht Oma: De Appel fallt nich wiet vun'n Stamm.
Third Example Sentence: Bi ehr Sturheit süht man, de Appel fallt nich wiet vun'n Stamm.

Idiom (Low Saxon): Nich lang snacken, Kopp in'n Nacken.
Syntactic Structure & Grammatical Form: Rhymed elliptical command; negated infinitival phrase followed by verbless imperative-like phrase.
Figurative Meaning (Contextualized Defin: Do not overthink or delay; get on with it immediately.
Non-Idiomatic Equivalent (Plain, Neutral: Snack nich so veel, fang nu an.
Usage Contexts: festive speech; drinking toasts; quick decisions; friendly dares
Cultural Origin or Historical Reference: Known in northern pub and celebration culture; the rhyme connects verbal brevity with immediate action.
First Example Sentence: Bi de Hochtiet rööp de Onkel: Nich lang snacken, Kopp in'n Nacken.
Second Example Sentence: De Suppe warrt koolt; nich lang snacken, Kopp in'n Nacken.
Third Example Sentence: As de Klock all teihn weer, sä Marie: Nich lang snacken, Kopp in'n Nacken.

Idiom (Low Saxon): Sik nich in de Bux maken.

Figurative Meaning (Contextualized Defin: Do not panic, be scared, or lose courage.
Non-Idiomatic Equivalent (Plain, Neutral: Hebb keen Angst un bliev ruhig.

First Example Sentence: Maak di nich in de Bux, de Hund bellt bloots.
Second Example Sentence: Vör de Prüfung muttst du di nich in de Bux maken.
Third Example Sentence: He maakt sik glieks in de Bux, wenn de Chef bloots kiekt.

Idiom (Low Saxon): Dat geiht mi op den Senkel.

Figurative Meaning (Contextualized Defin: That annoys me strongly or gets on my nerves.
Usage Contexts: complaints; customer service; family; social media; workplace frustration
Cultural Origin or Historical Reference: Senkel refers to a shoelace; the image of something constantly catching at one’s feet suits northern understated annoyance.
First Example Sentence: Dat ewige Tüdeln mit de App geiht mi op den Senkel.
Second Example Sentence: Wenn he jümmers to laat kummt, geiht mi dat op den Senkel.
Third Example Sentence: De piepende Döör geiht mi all siet Dagen op den Senkel.
